rv.q: And it makes its own gloriously off-kilter kind of sense.
Too many scenes feature two people arguing, and many of them end abruptly.
It’s characteristic of an evening that bubbles with sharp insights and yet somehow feels like less than the sum of its parts.
As a production it is imperfect but heroic in all it is trying to say about the way we live, how we might live differently and escape the toxicity of the digital world.
Overall, a mixed bag that ends strong.
Whether Martin Crimp’s witty but underpowered new version affords the best showcase for Oh’s abilities is another matter.
The result is a broad satire filled with platitudes and generalised debates about female empowerment, the patriarchy and trolls on the internet.
By the time the piece stumbles towards its meta conclusion at a baroque-themed costume party, we’ve long ceased to care about the outcome.

If Oh is the compelling heart of Rubasingham’s smartly directed entertainment, which is bright with laughter and then dips deeper into feeling, both are well served by designer Robert Jones, whose sets are as gorgeous as the costumes of the fancy-dress ball which triumphantly concludes the evening.
This is a Misanthrope full of interesting ideas and fine effects, but not quite enough bite or fury.

After that promising start, we’re introduced to Alice’s lover, the self-absorbed actor Stefan (Tom Mison) whose former problems with drinking and a professional need to be the centre of attention at all times, make him charmingly unbearable and equally unreliable.
But if there are plenty of current, provocative references here, they’re flimsily addressed and leave little to chew over once the story peters out.
The performances are good, the staging reasonable, and the storyline clever - but the spark is missing.

But the play just fizzles out and rather than a story with lots of hinge points, bringing together new information and insights, The Misanthrope becomes a series of conversations that barely hang together.
Scenes are full of conversations without purpose or substance.
Bringing new meaning to a rarely seen trope, you’d find it incredibly hard to hate The Misanthrope.
But the targets are rather scattergun later as the writing becomes somewhat unfocused.

But The Misanthrope is a play that flatters to deceive, filled to bursting with ideas it’s never quite able to unpack, a shiny bauble loaded with talent that’s just not quite as clever as it thinks it is.
The Misanthrope is a wonderfully fun piece that explores the human condition, asking questions about the world we live in and if we should perhaps be a bit nicer to our fellow planet dwellers.
Theatre’s take on The Misanthrope is worth seeing for the bravura opening that promised so much more laughter to come and for the twinkling drama of the closing scene.
Sandra Oh commands the stage as the misanthrope.

cn.t: Critics are mixed on Crimp's gender-flipped update of Molière's classic, praising Sandra Oh's fierce performance but finding the modernization uneven and punch-pulling, with sparkling verse that doesn't always land.
